intro: Brennan Park Recreation Centre on Centennial Way holds Squamish's arena and the aquatic centre. Residents have asked for years for more ice time and more pool space. The 2021 Brennan Park Fields and Lands Master Plan marks a future site for a second ice rink and an upgraded pool, but no money has been set aside to build either.

In December 2025 council funded a study of what Brennan Park needs next. A staff Recreation Centre Task Force, working with a consultant, is now looking at demand, costs, sites and ways to pay. Its final report is expected in spring 2027, and a new council will decide what, if anything, to build.
The pool side has an extra wrinkle: the aquatic centre is owned by the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District and run by the District of Squamish, so the regional district has a say in pool spending.
This ask is about what residents would most like to see added first.

facts.label: Study budget
facts.value: $125,000 for 2026, added to the financial plan in December 2025

facts.label: Funding to build
facts.value: None yet. Staff describe expansion projects as unfunded.

facts.label: Final report
facts.value: Expected in the second quarter of 2027. A "What We Heard" summary was planned for November 2026.

facts.label: Pool ownership
facts.value: The aquatic centre is owned by the Squamish-Lillooet Regional District and operated by the District

facts.label: Pool repair request for 2027
facts.value: $3.005 million in capital work on the existing pool, including $1.58 million for deck air handling equipment

facts.label: Existing arena
facts.value: $573,000 for arena air handling upgrades in 2027 and 2028, after a 2025 humidity problem made the ice unsafe

timeline.what: The Brennan Park Fields and Lands Master Plan goes to council. Its maps mark a future site for an upgraded pool and a second ice rink.
Council puts $125,000 for 2026 toward the Brennan Park upgrade study. A motion for $200,000 to study a second pool and rink by July 2026 fails.
Staff present the task force engagement plan, focused on interviews with user groups such as minor hockey, skating and swim clubs.
Council endorses the engagement plan and asks staff to report on a council committee to help shape the recommendation.
The draft 2027 to 2036 capital plan says the task force is in phase one of three.
The final task force report with options, costs and funding ideas is expected.

points: With one rink, hockey, figure skating and public skating all compete for the same hours. A second sheet would free up time for every group.
A 2025 shutdown of the only rink showed how exposed the town is when that one sheet of ice goes down.
Lessons, lane swimming, clubs and family swims all share one pool. More water would mean more lesson spots and more open swim time.
Swimming is a life skill and serves every age, from toddlers to seniors.

sides.answer: Both, even if taxes go up
points: Squamish is growing fast, and building both at once could save on design and site work compared with two separate projects.
Waiting only makes construction more expensive.
Neither project has money set aside, and the existing building still needs millions in repairs.
The task force study is not finished. Deciding before it reports could mean building the wrong thing.
Keeping the money free leaves room for other needs or lower tax increases.

questions.q: Has the District priced a second rink or pool?
questions.a: Not yet. The task force is preparing high level cost estimates, funding strategies and options, due in its final report in 2027.

The engagement plan focuses on interviews and a survey of user group members. It does not propose a new community wide survey, because the projects are unfunded and staff want to avoid false expectations.

questions.q: How did council vote on the study?
questions.a: The $125,000 study passed with Councillor Hamilton opposed. An earlier motion by Councillor Hamilton for $200,000 to study a second pool and rink failed, with Mayor Hurford and Councillors French, Andersen and Stoner opposed.
